summary: The walk gets its most lyrical and most argued chapter: be imitators of God as beloved children, walk in love as Christ loved and gave himself, walk as children of light — no immorality, no filthiness, no deceitful words, because the wrath comes on disobedience and everything exposed by the light is revealed. 'Awake, you who sleep.' Then the filling: don't be drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit — psalms, hymns, thanksgiving, submitting to one another in the fear of Christ. And then the household begins: wives to husbands as the assembly to Christ, husbands to wives as Christ to the assembly — love that gives itself, washes, nourishes; the one-flesh mystery; 'I speak concerning Christ and the assembly.'
whyItMatters: This chapter holds both the letter's most singable verses (5:2, 5:8, 5:14, 5:19-20) and its most debated passage (5:22-33). Reading it well means holding both: the light-walk that all traditions treasure, and the marriage passage that must be read whole — governed by mutual subjection, aimed at the great mystery of Christ and the assembly.

context.author: Paul, writing with the letter's liturgical register at full height — quoting what may be an early hymn ('Awake, you who sleep,' 5:14) and applying Genesis 2:24 to Christ and the assembly (5:31-32).
context.audience: The assembly as a worshiping household: the chapter addresses people who sing together (5:19) and people who are married or will be (5:22-33) — the same congregation, now told how the light-walk looks at table, in song, and in the most intimate room of the house.
context.date: Undated; the chapter's time-sense is 'the days are evil' (5:16) — redeeming the time is the response, not a date on a calendar.
context.setting: The same assemblies in a pagan city: sexual immorality and covetousness named as the ambient culture (5:3), drunkenness as the alternative to being filled (5:18), and the Roman household structure as the frame the letter instructs within.
context.literaryForm: Imperative chain turning to household code: love-light-wisdom triads (walk in love, walk as light, walk carefully), a contrast pair (drunk / filled), then paired addresses — wives/husbands — built around the Christ-assembly analogy and Genesis quotation.

outline.heading: Imitators of God, walking in love
outline.note: Be imitators as beloved children; walk in love as Christ's self-giving offering; no immorality, uncleanness, covetousness even named among you — no filthiness, foolish talking, jesting, but giving of thanks; the wrath of God comes on children of disobedience; do not partake with them.

outline.heading: Walking as children of light
outline.note: Once darkness, now light in the Lord — walk as children of light; the fruit of the light is goodness, righteousness, truth; no fellowship with the unfruitful deeds of darkness, but reprove them — everything revealed is light; 'Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'

outline.heading: Walking carefully, filled with the Spirit
outline.note: Watch carefully how you walk — redeem the time, understand the Lord's will; not drunk with wine but filled with the Spirit: psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, making melody in the heart, giving thanks always, subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ.

outline.heading: The household: wives and husbands
outline.note: Wives to husbands as to the Lord — the husband head as Christ head of the assembly; husbands love as Christ loved the assembly and gave himself — to sanctify, wash, present, nourish, cherish; 'the two will become one flesh'; 'this mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly'; each love, each respect.

keyVerses.text: Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children. Walk in love, even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance.
keyVerses.why: The chapter's standard in one breath: imitation defined not as copying power but as self-giving — the walk in love is Christ-shaped from the first verse.

keyVerses.text: Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit,
keyVerses.why: The letter's alternative to every empty filling: not controlled by wine but by the Spirit — and the evidence of the filling that follows is worship and mutual subjection, not private intensity.

keyVerses.text: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her,
keyVerses.why: The marriage passage's center of gravity: the husband's command is a cross-command — love defined by Christ's self-giving for the assembly, which sets the entire passage's tone.

questions.question: How can anyone 'imitate God'?
questions.answer: The chapter defines imitation immediately: 'Walk in love, even as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us' (5:2). The imitation is not of God's power or knowledge but of his self-giving — and it is the imitation 'as beloved children,' a family likeness learned from love received. The standard is stated as sacrifice: 'an offering and a sacrifice to God.'

questions.question: Why does Paul call covetousness idolatry (5:5)?
questions.answer: The chapter groups 'the covetous man' with the sexually immoral and the unclean and names him 'an idolater' (5:5). The logic is the one the whole Bible carries: what a person serves and trusts is their god — and greed installs a god of self. It is why the warning is about 'inheritance in the Kingdom of Christ and God': the covetous already have one.

questions.question: What does 'the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth' mean here?
questions.answer: The hosted text at 5:9 says the fruit of the light (some manuscripts say 'Spirit'; the WEB's footnote tradition reads 'light') is 'in all goodness and righteousness and truth.' In the chapter's flow, light produces a harvest: children of light prove 'what is well pleasing to the Lord' (5:10) by what grows — the triad matches the walk, not just the talk.

questions.question: Is 'Awake, you who sleep' (5:14) Paul's own words or a quotation?
questions.answer: The text introduces it with 'he says' — most readers take it as a quotation, perhaps from an early Christian hymn or baptismal song, blending Isaiah 60's light-rising language with resurrection. Paul cites it the way the letter cites Psalm 68 (4:8): as Scripture-shaped language the congregation already sings, now applied: 'arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.'

questions.question: 'Redeeming the time, because the days are evil' — redeem how?
questions.answer: The word is a marketplace word — buying up, making the most of. The chapter's own application surrounds the phrase: not walking as unwise but as wise, understanding 'what the will of the Lord is' (5:15-17). Evil days are not escaped by leaving the market but by buying well inside it — wisdom's purchases, not the fool's dissipation.

questions.question: What does being 'filled with the Spirit' look like in this chapter?
questions.answer: Not a private sensation: the verse's evidence is corporate worship and mutual deference — 'speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; giving thanks always... subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ' (5:19-21). The filling is measured in song, thanks, and the willingness to yield.

questions.question: How should the wives-and-husbands passage be read as a whole?
questions.answer: Start at 5:21, which the grammar ties to what follows: 'subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ' governs the whole household section. Then read the pairs in full: wives are addressed toward husbands 'as to the Lord' in a household structure the letter did not invent, and husbands are commanded to love 'as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her' — the longer, costlier command, aimed at the party with legal power in a Roman household. The passage ends by naming its true subject: 'This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly' (5:32). Readers differ genuinely over application today; the passage's own frame is mutual subjection, cross-shaped love, and the mystery.

questions.question: What is the 'washing of water with the word' in verse 26?
questions.answer: The husband's Christ-like love aims to sanctify and cleanse — 'having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word' (5:26). Most readers hear baptism (water) joined to proclamation (word); some read the word as the gospel that makes the washing meaningful. The verse's point in context is the aim of the love: the husband's self-giving serves the wife's holiness, not his own comfort — love that washes is the passage's test of the command.

questions.question: Why does Genesis 2:24 appear at the end — 'the two will become one flesh'?
questions.answer: Paul quotes the creation text and then interprets it in one of the letter's boldest moves: 'This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the assembly' (5:31-32). Marriage's one-flesh is treated as a live pointer to a greater union — the letter has been saying since 2:14-16 that Christ and his people are one body; here the marriage bed becomes the human picture of it. The quotation also grounds the passage in Scripture, not custom: the one-flesh is older than Rome.

glossary.def: The walk-identity of 5:8: once darkness, now light in the Lord — a changed nature, not just changed behavior.
Buying up the moment — marketplace language for wisdom's use of 'evil days' (5:16); the opposite of dissipation.
Genesis 2:24's phrase, quoted at 5:31 and applied to Christ and the assembly — the marriage union as the visible picture of the letter's greater union.
